newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope, Castro agree on papal trip to Cuba.
newsitem.headline: Pope, Castro agree on papal trip to Cuba.

text.p: Pope John Paul accepted an "unconditional" invitation from President Fidel Castro to visit communist Cuba next year during an historic meeting at the Vatican on Tuesday.
"The Pope accepted the invitation," chief Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls said after the 35-minute audience.
He said it was understood by both sides that there would be no limitations on what the Pope could say or where he could go during what will be his first trip to the Caribbean island.
"No precise date was fixed but the president and the Holy Father both said they hoped it could be carried out some time next year," Navarro-Valls said.
He defined the invitation as "concrete" and said it was clear that Castro, one of the world's last communist leaders, wanted the visit. Preparations would begin soon, he added.
Navarro-Valls would not be drawn on whether Castro and the Polish-born Pope, one of the key influences on the fall of communism in eastern Europe, had discussed human rights issues.
A statement said that Castro discussed political issues with Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Angelo Sodano.

"Holy Father, I hope to see you in Cuba soon," Navarro-Valls quoted Castro as telling the Pope at the end their meeting in the Pontiff's frescoed private study. The Pope replied: "Thank you, my blessings on the Cuban people."

The Pope and Castro, both major figures in 20th century history, talked privately in Spanish during the audience after the veteran revolutionary arrived at the Vatican under some of the heaviest security seen for a visiting head of state.
Cuba is the only Spanish-speaking country in Latin America which the Pope has not visited. He is due to travel to Brazil next October, when a Cuba visit could be added.
"Holy Father, this is a great honour for me," Castro, who was schooled by the Jesuits as a child, told the Pope as they met on the threshold of the papal study.

His visit, though billed as private, had all the trappings of a state visit to the Vatican including a 25-minute tour of St Peter's Basilica, Christendom's largest church, where one witness said Castro had "marvelled" at the art.
The Cuban leader also toured the Sistine Chapel and lunched with Vatican prelates who had previously visited Cuba.
They said he had pulled out photographs taken of himself with the Pope and had clearly been moved by the occasion.
"Castro said he judged his meeting with the Holy Father an extraordinary event and was very happy," one of the prelates, Archbishop Cipriano Calderon, told reporters.
Navarro-Valls said most of the audience dealt with the role of the Roman Catholic Church in Cuba, where relations with the state have been sometimes frosty.
"They examined questions concerning the normalisation of the conditions of existence of the Church in Cuba and in general the role of believers in Cuban national life," the spokesman said.

Shortly after Castro took control in 1959, Cuba was declared a socialist state. Some 350 Catholic schools were nationalised and more than 100 priests expelled. Freedom of worship and religious instruction are limited to church premises.
The restrictions on the Church now are similar to those in place in the Soviet Union and parts of eastern Europe until the collapse of the Iron Curtain.
Navarro-Valls said Castro discussed more political issues, such as "the development of Cuban society" and Cuba's position in the world, at a separate 45-minute meeting with Sodano.
The phrasing was an apparent reference to calls for democracy in Cuba and the 34-year-old U.S. embargo against the Caribbean island, which the Vatican has condemned several times.
Castro was whisked into the Vatican in a motorcade of 16 cars, one with a light machine gun poking through its sunroof.
All media access for the meeting, the Pope's most significant since he received then Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev in December 1989, was cancelled at an hour's notice.
